name: The Potawatomi camp of August 1812: the lodges at the creek's middle reach
aka: the Indian camp near the fort

grade.why: Known from maps or written records; no picture of it has been found.

documented_range.note: THE CAMP OF THE AUGUST GATHERING, DATED BY TWO EVENTS AND NOT BY A DAY IT WAS PITCHED. It opens on 12 August 1812: 'The Indians being assembled from the neighboring villages, a council was held with them on the afternoon of the 12th' (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII), so the gathering was camped by then; Heald's letter has them coming 'from all quarters' for the factory's goods, and nothing dates the first lodge, so the camp may be older than its range. It stood on the 14th, the scene date (Currey 1912 ch. III (lines 2239-2248), the view from the fort's walls on the evening of the last day, 14 August 1812: 'Toward the west was the Agency House, standing near the bank of the river, beyond which were the groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek that formerly flowed into the main stream at the present State Street.'), and on the 15th (Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Mrs. Helm's narrative of 15 August: led 'back towards the Chicago River, along the southern bank of which was the Pottowattamie encampment', to 'one of the wigwams', where water was dipped 'from a stream that flowed near' (Kinzie's footnote 36: 'Along the present State Street').). It closes on 16 August, the morning the fort was burned (Wau-Bun ch. XIX); when the gathering broke up after that no source read here says, and the 16th is the bound this project chose. Nothing of 1835 can draw it. T-2515; the groups rebuilt by T-3342.

change_note: A ground of the Potawatomi camp of the August 1812 gathering on the State Street creek: the lodges at the creek's middle reach. Rebuilt by T-3342 as a working camp, flagged for review.

placement.position_note: THE PLACE IS THE SOURCES', THE SPOT IS OURS. Currey puts the Potawatomi's habitual camping place at the creek or swale that opened into the river at the later State Street bridge (Currey 1912 ch. II (Gutenberg #52346 plain text, lines 1360-1365): 'their favorite camping place being at a point on the south bank near the present State Street bridge. A swale or gully opened into the river there, reaching back as far as the present line of Randolph Street.'), and the gathering's lodges there on the scene date (ch. III, 'clustered along the creek'); Wau-Bun puts the encampment on the river's south bank with a stream beside it. The committed 1812 ground carries that creek as the state_slough_course and state_slough_mouth swales. So the camp is drawn on the creek's banks, never in its bed, in six grounds along its course (with the other potawatomi_camp_1812_* records). On the creek's south-east bank where it bends west, about 190 m above its mouth: local E +752..+788, N -190..-162. This ground is the largest working group, two arbors to its yards. Which bank, how far apart and where each rectangle sits are this project's (T-3342), chosen on level ground: measured on the e1830_natural heightfield its outline lies between -0.02 and +0.11 m of the origin's 0.84 m (the walker's tolerance is 0.35 m), and it stands 4.9 m from the swale's cut. Nothing else of 1812 stands on it; the 1835 town's footprints that later cover parts of it never stand on the same date. The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 0. L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515.

canoe_edge.note: No canoes in this group. L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515.

mat_condition.note: The mats' condition: new ones fresh and golden, weathered ones greyed by seasons of carrying and rain, mixed both. Which group has which is this project's. L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515.

function.note: The camp of the Potawatomi gathered at Chicago in August 1812, before the evacuation of the fort: Wau-Bun's 'Pottowattamie encampment' on the river's south bank (ch. XIX) and Currey's 'groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek' on 14 August (ch. III). Heald's letter says they came in for the goods of the factory store; Wau-Bun's council of the 12th was held with them. Whose lodges these were the sources do not say lodge by lodge — Wau-Bun names the wife of Wau-bee-nee-mah, 'a chief from the Illinois River', standing at one wigwam — and no lodge here is given to a family, a band or a person.

occupants.value: Nobody this layer names or counts. The camp stands for the families of the gathering, whom no roll counts; no household card is minted for it and no name, band or person is given to any lodge. No figure is drawn (L1).
occupants.note: Seats nobody: see the value. T-2515.

citations.citation: J. Seymour Currey, The Story of Old Fort Dearborn. Chicago: A. C. McClurg & Co., 1912 (published August 1912). A popular history of the first fort from 1803 to its burning in 1812, compiled from the printed accounts and the pioneer recollections before it, with eleven illustrations.

a 'Map of Chicago in 1812' facing p. 165, not yet opened
the Lee family's house near the fort, on the river bank opposite the mouth, near the later Madison Street and Michigan Avenue, with the sand-bar as the reason (lines 1456-1463)
the Burns house, John Burns's cabin on the north bank near the later State Street bridge, west of the Kinzies' (lines 1565-1576, 2249-2251, 2820-2822)

research_note: THIS RECORD IS FLAGGED review_required, AND touches_removal, because it builds the camp of the Potawatomi gathered at Chicago on the eve of 15 August 1812 — the people whose land this was and who were removed from it in 1835 — from accounts written by the garrison's side, settler historians and an agent among their neighbours. The owner's rulings of 2026-10-16 (AGENTS.md § Standing constraint) trust this project to draw Native depictions on fair and reasonable judgement and lift the hold the flags once put on the scene's release; the flags stay, and say why here. WHAT IS DRAWN (T-3342, rebuilt from the T-2515 group of identical domes at the owner's ask of 2026-11-03): a working camp of families in late summer — mat lodges of several sizes and a long lodge, lodges roofed in elm bark, bark houses, bough arbors over the cooking, hearths with kettles and spits, drying racks, storage scaffolds, hide frames, firewood, mortars, canoes drawn up by the water and a horse ground with tether stakes and pack saddles — each read from the nearest accounts of the Potawatomi and their neighbours on the western lakes (Forsyth c. 1827 in Blair 1912; Wau-Bun; Hubbard 1911; Skinner 1927, from Prairie Potawatomi narrators), none described at Chicago. NOTHING IS STAGED: no figure, no flame or smoke above a hearth's coals, no ceremony, no council, no dialogue and nothing of the next morning; no sacred bundle, society lodge, sweat lodge or women's lodge is drawn, and no lodge is given to a family, a band or a person. WHAT WOULD REPLACE THIS: a source that counts or maps the lodges of August 1812, pictures one, or places the camp on the creek more exactly; any of them would move, re-form or retire these groups. L-1812-potawatomi-camp-2515.
